lines.note: Horiume means filling by digging, as with a ditch. Its actual first row was clipped by the old geometry; the replacement crop now shows the whole definition and column boundary.
Horiokoshi is digging something out or uprooting it. Arran- begins arrancar, and the historical oita ending is retained.
Stones are the objects extracted by digging. Car completes arrancar from the preceding row, not a new Portuguese noun.
Horiuzume is burying or covering over. The compound combines excavation with filling; uru and eta are the printed inflectional endings.
Com terra specifies covering with earth. The short line remains the completion of horiuzume's definition.
Horiuzumi is a related verbal form with mu and unda endings. Idem refers to the preceding burying sense rather than requiring its whole gloss to be repeated.

runs.text: Certa diuiſa de que vſão na guerra como

lines.note: Horo is a military identifying device. The Portuguese account describes its form in the next row, rather than treating foro as Portuguese jurisdiction.

runs.text: pauelhanſinho que leuão os ſoldados nas coſtas.

lines.note: It resembles a small pavilion carried on soldiers' backs. Pauelhanſinho is the historical diminutive; do not normalize it to a modern spelling.
Horo o kakuru is putting this device on one's back. Some strokes of Forouo are worn, but the repeated headword and verb fit the visible text.
Horobi, horoburu, is intransitive destruction or ruin. The examples begin houses and a kingdom; rei- continues reino below.
The kingdom example closes, and Permet. introduces a figurative sense. Hito no shin- begins the example concerning a person's estate.
Shindai ga horoburu means one's estate or means falling into ruin. The cross-line shin/dai sequence is Japanese 身代 in context, not the modern sense of a bed frame.
Horobiuse intensifies the destruction to disappearance. The older use/suru inflection is kept as printed rather than replaced by a modern paradigm.
Nothing remains, or it comes to an end. Acabarſe is visible and grammatical; OCR acaba ſe dropped the r and split the infinitive.
Horoboshi is transitive, destroying something, contrasting with horobi. The Portuguese destruir/desfazer supports that opposition.
Hōroku is glossed takara, takara, wealth. The repeated gloss is actually printed and should not be deduplicated as an apparent copying error.
The homophonous hōroku is an earthenware pot. The circumflex spelling is retained independently of the unrelated wealth sense.
Hōroku-tsukuri is a potter, literally a maker of the pots just defined. The compound boundary is a reading aid, not punctuation added to the original.
Horohoroto describes loosening or unrolling. Adu. is italic, and the reduplicated form belongs to a cluster of mimetic expressions rather than the verb horu, dig.

runs.text: ou deſennouelar algum fio, ou deſe ſoltarem os

lines.note: Thread unwinds and hair comes loose. Desennouelar is the historical Portuguese verb; its unfamiliar appearance alone is not evidence of an OCR error.

runs.text: cabelos, ou deſe deſapegar a era daruore, &c.

lines.note: Ivy detaching from a tree is another example. Era is the printed spelling for the plant, corresponding to modern hera, not the noun meaning an era.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Modo de ſe quebrar, ou esboroar al

lines.note: The adverb also describes breaking or crumbling. The separately detected pilcrow belongs to this physical row and is retained in its widened crop.

runs.text: gũa couſa como parede de barro, &c. ¶

lines.note: A clay wall is an example of something crumbling. Couſa, not OCR couſo, is visible; Na- begins namida in the following Japanese example.
Namida ga horohoroto ochita describes tears falling freely. The initial Na- comes from the prior row; Cairão is retained as the historical printed past-form spelling in this context.
The tears fall in a stream; then kazura introduces a creeper or vine example. Its zzu spelling should not be reduced to a modern romanization.
Toki hirogareba describes the vine loosening and spreading. The worn e before ba is supported by enlargement and the conditional form; OCR firogaroba produced an anomalous ending.
The Portuguese completes the ivy's loosening and spreading. Eſtendendoſe expresses the latter action and belongs to the preceding Japanese clause.
Horomeki describes rice separating or crumbling. The scan ends arroz with a comma, not the OCR period; the description continues immediately below.

runs.text: &c. que não he viſcoſo, ou eſboroarſe, ou eſ

lines.note: The rice is not sticky; the sense also covers crumbling or breaking small. The enlarged right margin contains no separate dash after eſ, so the OCR's trailing hyphen is removed.
Miuçarſe completes eſmiuçarſe, becoming small fragments. The noun is couſa; OCR coula confused long s with l.

Horomiso is a kind of miso, italic here in the Portuguese explanation. The far-right (leis. is a physically displaced completion of the next row's hōron definition; it is retained here and not duplicated as an invented row below.

Hōron, nori o ronzuru, is debate about laws or doctrine. Its Portuguese completion leis. is printed up on c1-l031 after a displacement mark; obsolete duplicate c1-l033 was removed without renumbering later stable IDs.
Horoke means breaking or crumbling apart. This is the next physical row after hōron, confirming that no separate leis row intervenes.
Horoketa nari describes a disheveled appearance. Nari concerns outward form or dress, not a copular ending that needs to be silently separated.

runs.text: hum andar mal vestido, ou roto.

lines.note: The person is badly dressed or in torn clothes. Roto is the garment-related condition here, clarifying the figurative extension from crumbling.
Hororihororito is another mimetic adverb for falling apart. The scan has desfa-, not OCR desfu-, beginning desfazer.

runs.text: zer, ou esboroar algũa couſa. ¶ Itẽ, Mo

lines.note: Zer completes desfazer; esboroar describes crumbling. The scan supports b rather than OCR h in eshoroar; Mo begins modo below.

runs.text: do de cairem as lagrimas dos olhos.

lines.note: The adverb can also describe tears falling from the eyes. This repeats a related sense, but it is genuine dictionary text rather than duplicate OCR to remove.
Hororito has the same senses. Dōshin ga vo- begins an example of a religious inclination arising; the split belongs to okotta below.
Okotta completes the Japanese verb. The Portuguese says being tenderly moved to devotion; its à is visibly accented, and the historical deuação spelling is retained.

runs.text: Eſtrepito das aſas da galinha do ma-

lines.note: Hororo is the noise of a wild bird's wings. Ma- begins mato; the description is narrowed to a pheasant by the following Japanese name.
Hororo o utsu is making that wing-beating sound. Eſtre continues eſtrepito without adding a hyphen not supported by the scan.

runs.text: pito, ou ſom o Quiji quando bate as aſas.

lines.note: Quiji, kiji, is the pheasant beating its wings. The Japanese bird name is visibly roman inside the italic Portuguese sentence; its text is retained but its run styling is corrected.
Hosa is a particular dignity or office. The concise gloss does not warrant choosing a modern administrative equivalent without further evidence.
Hosa no kenpei refers back to hosa. Qenpei represents kenpei, and the final i introduces the equivalence rather than being part of the title.
Hōsaki denotes the prominent cheeks. Tight enlargement resolves the accent as a circumflex, also recorded in NINJAL Fôsaqi; the headword is not the unrelated plain hosaki, tip.

runs.text: Fǒſat. Cǒbaxij fuda. i, Fǒcan, l, fǒbocu.

lines.note: Hōsat is an honorific for an elegant letter, with kōbashii fuda as its gloss. Enlargement recovers xij and the damaged f/d in Cǒbaxij fuda, not OCR Cǒbai i, ſuca; the explanation continues in column 2.

runs.text: Palaura pera louuar a carta eſcrita elegante-

lines.note: The hōsat expression from the previous column praises an elegantly written letter. Elegante- continues elegantly on the next row; the noun being praised is carta.

runs.text: mente honrando a peßoa que eſcreueo.

lines.note: Mente completes elegantemente; the expression honors the writer. Peßoa retains its joined double-s glyph rather than being recast as two long s letters.
Hōso denotes royal dignity. The circumflex and the unaccented final o are retained from the visible headword, independently of adjacent hōsō words.
Hōsō is fragrant grass, kōbashii kusa. Both carons are visible, and S marks the written-register expression.
The next hōsō denotes smallpox or the pox disease described by bexigas. The shared romanization does not make the botanical and disease entries duplicates.
Hōsō, toma no mado, is a window through a mat covering. Both circumflexes are visible; the Japanese paraphrase differentiates it from the preceding caron forms.

runs.text: Fune entre as tomas, ou eſteiras com que ſe

lines.note: The opening is in the mats covering a boat. Fune and tomas are Japanese-derived terms inside the Portuguese explanation, visibly italic here; keep the scan's typefaces.
Cobre completes the description of the covering. This short word is a verb here, not Portuguese cobre meaning copper.

runs.text: No Cami ſe diz feſo. Embigo.

lines.note: Hoso means navel; in Cami the term is heso. The italic feſo is genuine Japanese embedded in the explanatory sentence, not an unrecognized Portuguese word.

runs.text: Lugar eſtreito entre duas caſas como

lines.note: Hosoai is a narrow space between two houses. The following azinhaga gives a lane as an example rather than a separate sense of ai.
Azinhaga is a narrow lane. The short continuation belongs to hosoai and remains distinct from the next cord entry.
Hosobiki is a linen cord. The q in biqi gives ki; the scan does not support normalizing it to a modern alphabetic spelling.
Hosokubi means the neck. The Portuguese peſcoço confirms kubi, with no need to add an adjective that the original gloss does not contain.
Hosohibo, or hosohibo no ito, is a silk term. The scan repeats fibo in the expanded name; OCR foſonbono lost that sequence. NINJAL independently corroborates the repeated compound.

runs.text: lho, boa, & feita em fardo de Iapão.

lines.note: Lho completes atilho, describing silk without binding, of good quality and packed as a Japanese bale. The historical wording is retained rather than recast as modern textile terminology.

runs.text: Cinta, ou lugar por onde cingem

lines.note: Hosogoshi is the waist, where a belt is tied. Voiced goxi corresponds to koshi in a compound and is not a mistaken g for q.
O cinto completes the belt description. It is the object of cingem on the preceding row, not a new dictionary definition.

runs.text: Vaſo como gumil em que metem

lines.note: Hosoguchi is a narrow-mouthed vessel resembling a gumil. The Portuguese establishes a container, while the Japanese compound points to its narrow opening.
Fragrant herbs or flowers are placed in the vessel. Chiroſas is retained as printed; no e is inserted solely to match modern cheiroſas.
Hosoi means thin and long, with thread as an example. Li- continues linha, not the Japanese syllable ri.
Nha completes linha. This row closes the adjective's gloss before its separately indented derived forms.
Hososa is the nominal form, thinness. It is printed as its own indented physical row; there is no missing Portuguese translation to invent.
Hosō is the adverbial contracted form of hosoi. Its accent is retained, and its separate physical row is preserved alongside hososa.
Hosoiri denotes a sneaking or concealed thief. The scan supports eſcõdido, with õ rather than OCR ã; the Portuguese word and visible round vowel agree.
Hosomari is becoming thinner. It is intransitive, contrasting with the following hosome, and its printed atta ending is retained.
Hosome means making something thin or small. The transitive Portuguese adelgaçar/fazer distinguishes it from hosomari.
Kuchi o hosomuru is making the mouth small. The older verb form is supported by the example and should not be modernized to hosomeru in Level 1.

runs.text: a boca pequena como quẽ quer aſuuiar. ¶

lines.note: The lips are narrowed as for whistling. Aſuuiar is the historical Portuguese form, not an OCR spelling to replace automatically.
The same Japanese expression is used metaphorically. Per met. is an explanatory label, while kuchi o hosomuru remains roman.

runs.text: tar a mão não dando tanto como primeiro.

lines.note: The metaphor is becoming less generous, giving less than before. Apertar a mão explains tightening expenditure rather than literal mouth shape.
Hosomichi is a narrow path. This transparent compound connects hosoi with michi, confirming the consonant reading.
Hosomono is glossed gold. That is a specialized lexical sense: do not replace the clear Ouro merely because the compound literally suggests fine or thin things.
Hosonagai means slender and long. The two adjectives in Portuguese map directly to the compound's components.
Hoso no o and heso no o denote the umbilical cord. Tripa is Portuguese, including its capital T; the OCR's isolated roman T is restyled with the italic definition.

runs.text: o menino no embigo quando nace.

lines.note: The cord is attached to the newborn's navel. Nace is the printed historical form, not silently expanded to nasce.
Hososuji, also hososujina, describes something long and narrow. Gi here belongs to the historical ji spelling, not modern gi; the generated kana must be interpreted accordingly.
Hososujina katana is the example. The Japanese phrase is roman, while Ca- begins the Portuguese borrowed noun's translation below.
The sword has a narrow blade. The borrowed catana is italic across the Ca-/tana boundary, unlike its roman occurrence inside the Japanese example.
Hosoutsubo is a small quiver. Tç represents ts; the plain initial hoso component should not acquire a long-vowel accent from surrounding Sino-Japanese words.
Hosoya is a small arrow. The definition then adds a pragmatic explanation: the expression often minimizes one's own possession.
The speaker refers humbly to himself. The scan supports deſi, de si, not OCR deji; this is Portuguese reflexive wording, not a Japanese syllable.
The thing minimized is the speaker's arrow. The diminutive interpretation belongs to the honorific context, not a claim about the arrow's actual dimensions.

runs.text: Quantidade, ou medida de meo dedo em

lines.note: Hōsun is a square measure described as half a finger. The caron is retained; a modern numerical conversion would go beyond this transcription note.
Em quadro is completed here, specifying a square measure. Quadro is not an independent picture or frame entry.
Hossō is the Buddhist sect. Two long-s stems are visible where OCR read ſt; Foſſǒ is also corroborated by NINJAL's lexical form Fossǒ.
Hossoku is laws or ordinances, glossed nori, nori. The repeated Japanese gloss is intentional print and remains; the roman double long s is not the italic ß convention.
Another hossoku, preferably hassoku, means setting out. Potiùs is wholly italic, not alternating isolated letters; the scan shows two s stems in Foſſocu where OCR omitted one.
Catchword repeating ſu. at the beginning of f214. The phrase ashi wo okosu continues there; this bottom-right repetition is furniture, not a second body syllable. Its stable ID is retained.
